title: Jaxon Smith‑Njigba’s Stifling Defense Powers Seahawks to End Chiefs’ Winning Streak
body:
Seattle’s defense and the emergence of rookie wideout Jaxon Smith‑Njigba proved too much for the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday, handing the defending Super Bowl champions their first loss of the 2026 season. The Seahawks, who have relied on a stout unit and a balanced offense all year, out‑performed Kansas City in every phase, snapping the Chiefs’ early‑season unbeaten streak and reaffirming Seattle’s status as a legitimate contender in the NFC West.  

The game’s turning point came in the third quarter when Smith‑Njigba, the former Ohio State standout, hauled in a 38‑yard touchdown that put Seattle ahead 21‑10. The play showcased his route‑running precision and the chemistry he has quickly built with quarterback Geno Smith, who threw for 285 yards and three touchdowns. Smith‑Njigba’s performance was a stark contrast to the Chiefs’ offense, which has been anchored by Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes since his trade to Seattle last offseason. Mahomes, limited to 212 passing yards and a single touchdown, was repeatedly pressured by Seattle’s aggressive front seven, which recorded four sacks and forced two turnovers.  

Seattle’s defensive success was not accidental. Defensive coordinator Kris Rogers has re‑engineered the secondary, emphasizing press coverage and disguised blitzes that confused Chiefs’ quarterback reads. Cornerback Ahkello Holmes delivered a pick‑six in the second quarter, extending the Seahawks’ lead and shifting momentum. Linebacker Jordyn Brock, returning from a preseason injury, posted a career‑high 12 tackles and a strip‑sack that set up the decisive field goal in the fourth quarter. The unit’s ability to limit Mahomes’ deep throws—holding him to a 45‑yard completion rate—underscored a strategic shift from the Seahawks’ traditionally run‑first identity to a more versatile, attack‑oriented defense.  

The loss also highlighted the Chiefs’ lingering adjustments after the high‑profile trade that sent Mahomes to Seattle in exchange for a package of draft picks and a future first‑rounder. While Mahomes’ presence has undeniably elevated Seattle’s offensive ceiling, the Chiefs appear to be grappling with a new identity without their longtime leader. Head coach Andy Reid emphasized that the team is “still finding its rhythm” and will need to lean on veteran playmakers like Travis Kelce and the emerging talent of rookie running back Jaxon Brown to re‑establish a balanced attack.  

For Seattle, the victory is a statement win that validates the front office’s aggressive offseason moves. General manager John Sullivan, who orchestrated the Mahomes acquisition, now has an AP Offensive Player of the Year in Smith‑Njigba and a defense that can dictate terms against elite offenses. The Seahawks have improved to 2‑1, while the Chiefs fall to 1‑2, a rare blemish for a franchise that has not missed the playoffs in over a decade.  

Looking ahead, both teams face pivotal stretch‑run schedules. Seattle will host the Los Angeles Rams next week, a matchup that will test whether its defense can sustain pressure against a high‑octane passing attack. The Chiefs, meanwhile, travel to Denver, where altitude and a stout Broncos defense could further expose their offensive growing pains. If the Seahawks can maintain their defensive intensity and continue to integrate Smith‑Njigba into the offense, they could position themselves as early favorites in the NFC West race. Conversely, Kansas City must adapt quickly, finding new ways to protect Mahomes and re‑establish a winning formula, or risk falling behind in a fiercely competitive AFC West. The season is still young, but Sunday’s upset may prove to be a defining moment for both franchises.
